title: How to think like a strategic genius (5d thinking)
summary: The article argues that thinking ability—not IQ—determines life outcomes, and that smart people often fail because they think in limited, one-dimensional ways. It proposes a framework progressing from instinctual to generative levels of thinking, arranged across lines (domains), levels (cognitive depth), and altitude (cross-domain integration). Genius thinking is defined as the capacity to continue thinking beyond dogma, hold contradictory ideas, and traverse multiple knowledge domains without closing off inquiry.
central_argument: Your ability to continue thinking rather than prematurely close your mind at the limits of your current knowledge determines the outcomes available to you in life.
key_claims: Smart people are most likely to think like idiots because they stop thinking too early and defend pre-programmed answers.
Stupid thinking is one-dimensional, reductionistic, tribal, and closes off inquiry once it reaches what it believes is truth.
Knowing is horizontal (domain expertise) while understanding is vertical (cognitive operating system sophistication).
The 'smart but dumb' phenomenon results from horizontal advancement in one domain paired with vertical cognitive stagnation.
There are five levels of cognitive development: instinctual, conformist, individualist, synthesist, and generative.
First-tier thinking (levels 1-2) is dogmatic; second-tier thinking (levels 3-4) rejects dogma and seeks truth across perspectives.
Genius thinking is the ability to notice when your mind feels threatened and remain open to new perspectives rather than defend your position.
key_tensions: High IQ does not correlate with life success or happiness; many intelligent people fail while less intelligent people flourish.
Domain expertise (knowing a lot) can trap you in a bubble that prevents you from solving problems outside that domain.
First-principles thinking and systems thinking (standard frameworks) are insufficient without addressing how you continue to think beyond initial conclusions.
